extraction.name: Microsoft Common Objects in COntext (MS COCO)
extraction.description: A large-scale image dataset for recognizing, detecting, and segmenting common objects in complex everyday scenes in their natural context. The full collection contains 328,000 images, 91 proposed object categories, and 2.5 million labeled object instances, with per-instance segmentation annotations and five written captions per image. The 2014 release includes segmentation masks for 80 categories.
extraction.creator: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, Piotr Dollár
extraction.citeAs: Tsung-Yi Lin, Michael Maire, Serge Belongie, Lubomir Bourdev, Ross Girshick, James Hays, Pietro Perona, Deva Ramanan, C. Lawrence Zitnick, and Piotr Dollár. Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context. arXiv:1405.0312v3 [cs.CV], 21 February 2015.
extraction.isLiveDataset: The paper states that MS COCO will evolve and grow over time, with up-to-date information available on the project website.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Candidate object categories were compiled from existing category lists, frequently used words denoting visually identifiable objects, and objects named by children aged 4–8 in indoor and outdoor environments. Co-authors rated 272 candidate categories on a 1–5 scale, considering frequency, practical usefulness, and diversity, and selected 91 categories while balancing super-categories and retaining all PASCAL VOC categories. Images were collected from Flickr using object-object and object-scene search pairs to obtain non-iconic scenes. Single-category searches were used when necessary. At most five photographs taken by a single photographer within a short time window were downloaded. Amazon Mechanical Turk workers filtered candidate images to remove invalid or iconic images.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Software Collection, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The 2014 release lacks segmentation annotations for 11 proposed categories: hat, shoe, and eyeglasses because of too many instances; mirror, window, door, and street sign because they were ambiguous and difficult to label; plate and desk because of confusion with bowl and dining table; and blender and hair brush because of too few instances. In densely populated images, remaining instances after approximately 10–15 individual segmentations were labeled collectively as crowds rather than individually segmented.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Photographs uploaded to Flickr by amateur photographers, with searchable metadata, keywords, and text captions. The paper notes that these captions may be inaccurate.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For preliminary bounding-box detection experiments, tight-fitting bounding boxes were derived from annotated segmentation masks for a subset of 55,000 images.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: AMT workers removed invalid or iconic images from grids of candidate photographs. Near-duplicate images were explicitly removed using the method referenced in the paper, and images were grouped by photographer and date taken to minimize near duplicates across training, validation, and testing splits.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: AMT workers annotated images through category labeling, instance spotting, instance segmentation, segmentation verification, and crowd labeling. Category labeling used 11 super-categories, with workers dragging category icons onto one corresponding instance. Eight workers labeled each image. Instance spotting used eight workers, each marking up to ten instances of a category, aided by a previously identified instance and a magnifying-glass feature. A single worker segmented each object instance after passing a category-specific training task requiring agreement with ground truth. Three to five workers verified each segmentation. Poor segmentations were discarded and their instances returned for reannotation; all work from consistently poor workers was discarded. Dense groups were annotated with collective crowd masks. Five written captions were added to each image, with collection details deferred to a separate publication.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Amazon Mechanical Turk, using custom interfaces for filtering, category labeling, instance spotting, segmentation, verification, and crowd labeling. The instance segmentation interface was modified from OpenSurfaces source code.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Category presence was determined by the union of eight workers' responses to maximize recall; false positives were addressed in later stages. Worker precision and recall were compared with seven expert co-authors, using expert majority vote as ground truth. The union of eight AMT workers achieved higher recall than any individual expert; the authors estimated that over 99% of categories not subsequently rejected as false positives were detected. The paper discusses ambiguity in object presence and category definitions. A leave-one-out analysis assessed worker quality, and jobs from workers below the stated quality threshold were rejected. Segmentation verification began with three reviewers; any negative judgment triggered two additional reviews, after which at least four of five favorable votes were required. Sequential segmentation tasks ignored instance markers already covered by existing masks to resolve redundant instance annotations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Eight workers per image for category labeling; eight workers per image for instance spotting; one worker per object-instance segmentation; three reviewers per segmentation initially, increased to five if any initial reviewer rejected it; five written captions per image.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The first half of the dataset was released in 2014, with the second half planned for 2015. The 2014 release contains 82,783 training, 40,504 validation, and 40,775 testing images. The cumulative 2015 release was planned to contain 165,482 training, 81,208 validation, and 81,434 testing images. Training and validation annotations would be released, but test annotations would not. An automatic test evaluation server was being finalized. The authors were exploring additional annotation types and potentially adding segmentations for some omitted categories. Updated information would be provided on the project website.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Collection deliberately favors non-iconic images with multiple objects and rich contextual relationships, using paired object and scene queries. Category selection favors common, practically useful, diverse entry-level objects, balances super-categories, and retains PASCAL VOC categories for compatibility. Only 'thing' categories were included, not 'stuff' categories. Categories for which obtaining more than 5,000 instances was difficult were removed during selection.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Annotations focus on entry-level 'thing' categories rather than 'stuff,' fine-grained categories, or object parts. The 2014 release provides segmentations for only 80 of the 91 proposed categories. Object presence and category definitions can be ambiguous, and densely grouped objects are represented by crowd masks rather than complete individual-instance annotations. The paper notes that difficult non-iconic training examples may act as noise when models cannot capture their appearance variability. Reported preliminary detection experiments preceded the final dataset splits, and final test-set baselines were deferred until completion of the evaluation server.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing for object recognition, bounding-box detection, instance segmentation, precise 2D localization, contextual reasoning, and scene understanding, particularly for non-iconic objects in natural environments. Five captions per image support written image descriptions. Training and validation annotations are released, while test annotations are withheld for server-based evaluation. Crowd regions are ignored during detector evaluation and do not affect detector scores.
